title: Why Railways Used Wigwag on Bridges
topic: Why the 19th‑century British railway company installed “wigwag” signals on bridges (England, 1868)

lines: A signalman waved a giant flag from a rickety bridge, arms trembling.
His fellow engineers snorted, saying the ordinary semaphore arm would suffice.
They claimed a flag was old‑fashioned and useless.
A freight train roared toward the river, driver squinting at the arm.
Thick fog rolled in, hiding the semaphore like a ghost.
The driver could not tell if the line was clear.
You see, it’s like reading a street sign through a rain‑soaked windshield.
Wigwag uses one flag swung side‑to‑side, visible farther than a static arm.
From the bridge the driver’s eye meets the flag, not the arm.
The flag stays visible even when fog or smoke blocks the semaphore.
Bridges often limited the height of semaphore arms, forcing a lower placement.
Ironically, the same flag later retired, becoming a museum relic.
Modern colour‑light signals never needed a hand‑held flag.
When electric lights arrived, the flag finally faded into history.

claims.claim: Wigwag uses a single large flag swung side‑to‑side, readable over greater distances than semaphore.
Signals mounted low on bridges stay in the driver’s eyeline and avoid obstruction.
